title: Database Normalization
misconceptions: Higher levels of normalization always increase query execution speed.
First Normal Form (1NF) simply means that a table has a primary key defined.
A production database should always be fully normalized to the highest form regardless of performance requirements.
Denormalization is always a bad design choice that reflects a failure to understand normalization theory.

rubric.text: Defines database normalization as the systematic process of structuring a relational database schema to reduce data redundancy and ensure data integrity.
Explains the three types of modification anomalies (insertion, update, and deletion anomalies) caused by unnormalized database schemas.
Defines functional dependency (X -> Y) as a constraint where a set of attributes X uniquely determines the value of attribute set Y.
Explains First Normal Form (1NF), requiring that each table cell contains atomic (indivisible) values and that repeating groups or arrays are eliminated.

Explains Second Normal Form (2NF), requiring a table to be in 1NF and ensuring that all non-prime attributes are fully functionally dependent on the entire candidate key, eliminating partial dependencies.
Explains Third Normal Form (3NF), requiring a table to be in 2NF and ensuring that no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
Explains Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF), describing it as a stricter version of 3NF where for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
Explains the concept of lossless-join decomposition, ensuring that breaking a relation into smaller relations does not generate spurious tuples when joined back.
Explains the trade-offs of denormalization, describing how intentional redundancy can improve read query performance at the cost of write complexity and storage.
